The **Bank of England (BoE)** is the [central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank") of the United Kingdom and the model on which most modern central banks have been based. Established in 1694 to act as the [English Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England")'s banker and debt manager, and still one of the bankers for the [government of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom"), it is the world's second oldest central bank, after [Sweden's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank") (1668).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-3) It is considered to be one of the world's ["Big Four" central banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Four_(banking)#International_use "Big Four (banking)").

The bank was privately owned by stockholders from its chartering in 1694 until its nationalisation in 1946 by the [Attlee ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attlee_ministry "Attlee ministry").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-4) In 1998 it became an independent public organisation, wholly owned by the [Treasury Solicitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasury_Solicitor "Treasury Solicitor") on behalf of the government,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-boe-foi-5) with a mandate to support the economic policies of the government of the day,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-6) but [independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank_independence "Central bank independence") in maintaining price stability.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-7) In the 21st century the bank took on increased responsibility for maintaining and monitoring [financial stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_stability "Financial stability") in the UK, and it increasingly functions as a statutory [regulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_regulation "Financial regulation").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEStability-8)

The bank's headquarters have been in London's main financial district, the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London"), since 1694, and on [Threadneedle Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threadneedle_Street "Threadneedle Street") since 1734. It is sometimes known as "The Old Lady of Threadneedle Street", a name taken from a satirical cartoon by [James Gillray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gillray "James Gillray") in 1797.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-9) The road junction outside is known as [Bank Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Junction "Bank Junction"). The bank is custodian to the official [gold reserves of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_reserves_of_the_United_Kingdom "Gold reserves of the United Kingdom").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-10)

## Functions

According to its [strapline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strapline "Strapline"), the bank's core purpose is 'promoting the good of the people of the United Kingdom by maintaining monetary and financial stability'.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEHomepage-11) This is achieved in a variety of ways:[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEAbout-12)

### Monetary stability

Stable prices and secure forms of payment are the two main criteria for monetary stability.

#### Stable prices

Stable prices are maintained by seeking to ensure that price increases meet the Government's inflation target. The bank aims to meet this target by adjusting the base [interest rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interest_rate "Interest rate") (known as the [bank rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_rate "Bank rate")), which is decided by the bank's [Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_Policy_Committee_(United_Kingdom) "Monetary Policy Committee (United Kingdom)"). (The MPC has devolved responsibility for managing [monetary policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_policy "Monetary policy"); [HM Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HM_Treasury "HM Treasury") has reserve powers to give orders to the committee "if they are required in the public interest and by extreme economic circumstances", but Parliament must endorse such orders within 28 days.)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-13)

As of 2024 the inflation target is 2%; if this target is missed the Governor is required to write an open letter to the [Chancellor of the Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer "Chancellor of the Exchequer") explaining the situation and proposing remedies.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-14) Other than setting the base interest rate, the main tool at the bank's disposal in this regard is [quantitative easing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_easing "Quantitative easing").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-15)

#### Secure forms of payment

The bank has a monopoly on the issue of [banknotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banknotes_of_the_pound_sterling "Banknotes of the pound sterling") in England and Wales and regulates the issuance of banknotes by commercial banks in Scotland and Northern Ireland. Scottish and Northern Irish banks retain the right to issue their own banknotes, but they must be backed one-for-one with deposits at the bank, excepting a few million pounds representing the value of notes they had in circulation in 1845.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-scot-ni-16)

In addition the bank supervises other [payment systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_systems "Payment systems"), acting as a [settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_(finance) "Settlement (finance)") agent and operating [Real-time gross settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-time_gross_settlement "Real-time gross settlement") systems including [CHAPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHAPS "CHAPS").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-17) In 2024 the bank was settling around £500 billion worth of payments between banks each day.

### Financial stability

Maintaining financial stability involves protecting the UK's savers, investors and borrowers against threats to the financial system as a whole.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEStability-8) Threats are detected by the bank's surveillance and [market intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_intelligence "Market intelligence") functions, and dealt with through financial and other operations (both at home and abroad). The majority of these safeguards were put in place in after the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"):

#### Regulation

In 2011 the bank's [Prudential Regulation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prudential_Regulation_Authority_(United_Kingdom) "Prudential Regulation Authority (United Kingdom)") was established to regulate and supervise all major banks, building societies, credit unions, insurers and investment firms in the UK ('[microprudential regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microprudential_regulation "Microprudential regulation")').[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-18) The bank also has a statutory supervisory role in relation to [financial market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_market "Financial market") infrastructures.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-19)

#### Risk management

At the same time, the bank's [Financial Policy Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Policy_Committee "Financial Policy Committee") (FPC) was set up to identify and monitor [risks in the financial system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systemic_risk "Systemic risk"), and to take appropriate action where necessary ('[macroprudential regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroprudential_regulation "Macroprudential regulation")'). The FPC publishes its findings (and actions taken) in a biannual Financial Stability Report.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-20)

#### Banking services

The bank provides [wholesale banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wholesale_banking "Wholesale banking") services to the UK Government (and to over a hundred overseas central banks).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEBankServ-21) It manages the UK's [Exchange Equalisation Account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchange_Equalisation_Account "Exchange Equalisation Account") on behalf of [HM Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HM_Treasury "HM Treasury") and it maintains the government's [Consolidated Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consolidated_Fund "Consolidated Fund") account.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-22) It also manages the country's [foreign exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_exchange_market "Foreign exchange market") reserves and is custodian of the UK's (and others') [gold reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_reserves "Gold reserves").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-23)

The bank also offers 'liquidity support and other services to banks and other financial institutions'.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEAbout-12)[Commercial banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_banks "Commercial banks") customarily keep a sizeable proportion of their [cash reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_reserves "Bank reserves") on [deposit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deposit_(finance) "Deposit (finance)") at the Bank of England. These [central bank reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank_reserves "Central bank reserves") are used by the banks to settle payments with one another;[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-24) (for this reason the Bank of England is sometimes called 'the bankers' bank').[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEHistFun-25) In exceptional circumstances, the Bank may act as the [lender of last resort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lender_of_last_resort "Lender of last resort") by extending credit when no other institution will.

As a regulator and central bank, the Bank of England has not offered consumer banking services for many years, but it still does manage some public-facing services (such as exchanging superseded bank notes).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Exchanging_for_an_individual_at_the_Bank_of_England_counter-26) Until 2017, Bank staff were entitled to open current accounts directly with the Bank of England and were given the unique sort code of 10–00–00.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Bank_of_England_to_close_personal_banking_service_for_employees-27)

#### Resolution

Under the terms of the [Banking Act 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banking_Act_2009 "Banking Act 2009") the bank is the UK's Resolution Authority for any bank or building society judged '[too big to fail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too_big_to_fail "Too big to fail")'; as such it is empowered to act in the event of a [bank failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_failure "Bank failure") 'to protect the UK's vital financial services and financial stability'.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-28)

### Historic services and responsibilities

Between 1715 and 1998, the Bank of England managed Government Stocks (which formed the bulk of the [national debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_debt "National debt")): the bank was responsible for issuing stocks to stockholders, paying dividends and maintaining a register of transfers;[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEHistFun-25) however in 1998, following the decision to grant the bank operational independence, responsibility for government debt management was transferred to a new [Debt Management Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt_Management_Office_(United_Kingdom) "Debt Management Office (United Kingdom)"), which also took over Exchequer cash management and responsibility for issuing Treasury bills from the bank in 2000.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-29)[Computershare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computershare "Computershare") took over as the registrar for UK Government bonds ([gilt-edged securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilt-edged_security "Gilt-edged security") or 'gilts') from the bank at the end of 2004. The bank, however, continues to act as [settlement agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_(finance) "Settlement (finance)") for the Debt Management Office and custodian of its [securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securities "Securities").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEBankServ-21)

Ever since its foundation in 1694, the bank had provided a [retail banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_banking "Retail banking") service for the Government; however in 2008 it decided to withdraw from offering these services, which are now provided by a range of other financial institutions and managed by the [Government Banking Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Banking_Service "Government Banking Service").

Until 2016, the bank provided personal banking services as a privilege for employees.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Bank_of_England_to_close_personal_banking_service_for_employees-27) Previously, the bank had maintained private and commercial accounts for all sorts of customers, including individuals, small businesses and public organisations; but a change of policy following the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War") saw the bank increasingly withdraw from this type of business to focus more clearly on its central banking role.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-30)

## History

### Founding

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Running_Cash_Note_-_Bank_of_England_Museum_-_Joy_of_Museums.jpg/250px-Running_Cash_Note_-_Bank_of_England_Museum_-_Joy_of_Museums.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Running_Cash_Note_-_Bank_of_England_Museum_-_Joy_of_Museums.jpg)

Handwritten banknote dated 1697, signed 'for the Governor and Company of the Bank of England' by 2nd Cashier Robert Hedges

Following the [Revolution of 1688](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glorious_Revolution "Glorious Revolution"), which brought [William III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_III_of_Great_Britain "William III of Great Britain") and [Mary II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_II "Mary II") jointly to the British throne, the establishment of a national bank came to fruition. During the [Nine Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Years'_War "Nine Years' War") (1688–1697), the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") was defeated by the [French Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Navy "French Navy") in the 1690 [Battle of Beachy Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Beachy_Head_(1690) "Battle of Beachy Head (1690)"), causing consternation in the government of [William III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_III_of_England "William III of England"). The English government decided to rebuild the Royal Navy into a force that was capable of challenging the French on equal terms; however, their ability to do so was hampered both by a lack of available public funds and the government's low credit. This lack of credit made it impossible for the English government to borrow the £1.5m that it wanted to use to expand the Royal Navy.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-31)

#### Concept

The idea of a public bank antedated its establishment by two decades. It was a topic of discussion and dispute in the 1670s and 1680s. [John Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke "John Locke") was an early supporter of the concept, and, once it was established, an early investor.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-32) In 1691, Scottish trader and banker [William Paterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Paterson_(banker) "William Paterson (banker)") had proposed establishing a national bank as a means of bolstering public finances.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-33) As he later wrote in his pamphlet _A Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England_ (1694):

> "...it was proposed some years ago that a publick transferrable Fund of Interest should be established by Parliament, and made convenient for the Receipts and Payments in and about the Cities of London and Westminster; and to constitute a Society of Money'd Men for the government thereof, who should be induced by their Interest to exchange for Money the Assignments upon the Fund, at every demand".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-PatersonGodfrey1694-34)

While his scheme was not immediately acted upon, it did provide the basis for the bank's first Charter and the legislation which made its establishment possible.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEHistFun-25)

Two other key figures in the bank's creation were [Charles Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Halifax "Charles Montagu, 1st Earl of Halifax"), the Member of Parliament for Maldon, who played a crucial role in steering the proposals through Parliament (and was afterwards appointed [Chancellor of the Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer "Chancellor of the Exchequer")); and [Michael Godfrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Godfrey "Michael Godfrey"), who helped persuade City financiers of its benefits (and was subsequently chosen to be the bank's first Deputy Governor).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEHistFun-25)

It has also been claimed (by [W. R. Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._R._Scott_(economist) "W. R. Scott (economist)"), among others)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BR54-35) that [William Phips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Phips "William Phips") played a timely, if incidental, role: his successful expedition to retrieve booty from a sunken Spanish [galleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galleon "Galleon") (the _Nuestra Señora de la Concepción_) helped create an ideal market for the bank's foundation: flooding the market with bullion and creating an enthusiasm for [joint-stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint-stock_company "Joint-stock company") ventures.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-36)

#### Legislation

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Charles_Montagu%2C_1st_Earl_of_Halifax_by_Sir_Godfrey_Kneller%2C_Bt.jpg/250px-Charles_Montagu%2C_1st_Earl_of_Halifax_by_Sir_Godfrey_Kneller%2C_Bt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Halifax_by_Sir_Godfrey_Kneller,_Bt.jpg)

[Charles Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Halifax "Charles Montagu, 1st Earl of Halifax") played a key role in devising the legislation for establishing the Bank and steering it through the House of Commons.

Paterson's proposal required the Government to set up a fund from which interest would be paid to the subscribers. It was decided that this would be provided for by income from [tonnage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonnage_and_poundage "Tonnage and poundage"), and certain other shipping [duties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duty_(tax) "Duty (tax)") routinely levied by HM [Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchequer "Exchequer"); therefore Parliament approved the bank's establishment by means of the [Tonnage Act 1694](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonnage_Act_1694 "Tonnage Act 1694"):[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-37)

> An Act for granting to theire Majesties severall Rates and Duties upon Tunnage of Shipps and Vessells and upon Beere Ale and other Liquors for secureing certaine Recompenses and Advantages in the said Act mentioned to such Persons as shall voluntarily advance the summe of Fifteen hundred thousand Pounds towards the carrying on the Warr against France.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BankAct1694-38)

To induce subscription to the loan, the subscribers were to be [incorporated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incorporation_(business) "Incorporation (business)") by the name of the **Governor and Company of the Bank of England**. Public finances were in such dire condition at the time[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-39) that the terms of the loan (as laid down in the Act of Parliament) were that it was to be serviced at a rate of 8% per annum; there was also a service charge of £4,000 per annum payable to the bank for the management of the loan.

The Act limited the subscribers' investment to a maximum of £10,000 each in the first instance, and £1,200,000 in total (it was envisaged that the Exchequer would raise the remaining £300,000 through other forms of borrowing).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BankAct1694-38)

#### Incorporation

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Bank_of_England_Charter_sealing_1694.jpg/250px-Bank_of_England_Charter_sealing_1694.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bank_of_England_Charter_sealing_1694.jpg)

_Sealing of the Bank of England Charter (1694)_, by Lady Jane Lindsay, 1905

The [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") of the Bank of England was granted on 27 July 1694, three months after the passing of the Act.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-40)

In the end the £1.2 million was raised in 12 days; 1,268 people subscribed. Their holdings were known as Bank Stock (Bank Stock continued to be held in private ownership until 1946 when the Bank of England was nationalised).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-41) The majority of the original subscribers were of 'the [mercantile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercantile "Mercantile") middle classes of London' (though [tradesmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tradesmen "Tradesmen") and [artisans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artisans "Artisans") also subscribed).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Kynaston2017-42) Most (more than two-thirds) contributed less than £1,000. As a proportion of the total amount raised, 25% came from '[esquires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esquire "Esquire")', 21% from merchants and 15% from titled [aristocrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocrats "Aristocrats"). Twelve per cent of the original subscribers were women.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Kynaston2017-42)[King William and Queen Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_and_Mary_of_England "William and Mary of England") (jointly) invested £10,000, the maximum permitted sum, as did a handful of others, including Sir [John Houblon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Houblon "John Houblon").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-43)

Investment in the navy duly took place. As a side effect, the huge industrial effort needed (including establishing [ironworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironworks "Ironworks") to make more nails and advances[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] in agriculture feeding the quadrupled strength of the navy) started to transform the economy. This helped the new [Kingdom of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain") – [England and Scotland were formally united in 1707](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707 "Acts of Union 1707") – to become powerful. The power of the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") made Britain the dominant world power in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-44)

#### Governance

The first Governor of the bank was [John Houblon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Houblon "John Houblon"), and the first Deputy Governor [Michael Godfrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Godfrey "Michael Godfrey"). (330 years later, in 1994, the bank would issue a [£50 note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England_%C2%A350_note "Bank of England £50 note") depicting Houblon to mark its [tercentenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tercentenary "Tercentenary").)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-45)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Running_Cash_Note_-_Bank_of_England_Museum_-_Joy_of_Museums_-_2.jpg/250px-Running_Cash_Note_-_Bank_of_England_Museum_-_Joy_of_Museums_-_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Running_Cash_Note_-_Bank_of_England_Museum_-_Joy_of_Museums_-_2.jpg)

An early Bank of England note, with [Britannia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britannia "Britannia") emblem, signed by the Chief Cashier, [Thomas Madockes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Madockes "Thomas Madockes"), and dated 1699

Governance was vested in the Governor, his Deputy and a 'Court' of 24 Directors (most of whom were [merchant bankers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_banker "Merchant banker") recruited from the city); the Directors were elected annually by a 'General Court' of all the Bank's registered stockholders (collectively known as 'the Proprietors'). The [common seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_seal "Company seal") of the Court of Directors, adopted on 30 July 1694, depicted '[Britannia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britannia "Britannia") sitting and looking on a Bank of mony'; Britannia has been the bank's emblem ever since.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-46)

The Court appointed three senior officers who, alongside the Governor and Deputy Governor, were responsible for its day-to-day running of the bank: the Secretary and Solicitor, the First Accomptant, and the First Cashier. Their successors, the Secretary, Chief Accountant, and [Chief Cashier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Cashier_of_the_Bank_of_England "Chief Cashier of the Bank of England"), continued to head up the main divisions of the bank's operations for the next 250 years: the Chief Cashier and the Chief Accountant had oversight of the 'cash side' and the 'stock side' of the bank, respectively, while the Secretary oversaw its internal administration.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Hennessy1992-47)

Besides these officers, the bank in 1694 was staffed by seventeen clerks and two doorkeepers.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEHistFun-25)

#### Premises

The bank initially did not have its own building, first opening on 1 August 1694 in [Mercers' Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercers'_Hall "Mercers' Hall") on [Cheapside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheapside "Cheapside"). This however was found to be too small and from 31 December 1694 the bank operated from [Grocers' Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grocers'_Hall "Grocers' Hall") (located then on [Poultry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poultry,_London "Poultry, London")), where it would remain for almost 40 years.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoE1794-1984-48) (Houblon had served as Master of the [Grocers' Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grocers'_Company "Grocers' Company") in 1690–1691.)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEHistFun-25)

#### Operation

The Act of Parliament prohibited the bank from trading in goods or merchandise of any kind, though it was allowed to deal in gold and silver [bullion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullion "Bullion"), and in [bills of exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bills_of_exchange "Bills of exchange").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Allen1828-49) Before very long, the bank was maximising its profits by issuing [banknotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banknotes "Banknotes"), taking [deposits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deposits "Deposits") and lending on [mortgages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgages "Mortgages").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Kynaston2017-42)

In its early days the bank made significant losses, not least by accepting [clipped coins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coin_clipping "Coin clipping") in exchange for its banknotes.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Allen1828-49) The establishment of a Land Bank (by [John Asgill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Asgill "John Asgill") and [Nicholas Barbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Barbon "Nicholas Barbon")) in 1695, and a currency shortage occasioned by the [Great Recoinage of 1696](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recoinage_of_1696 "Great Recoinage of 1696"), both threatened the bank's position;[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEHistFun-25) but Parliament intervened, passing [another Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England_Act_1696 "Bank of England Act 1696") that year, which authorised the bank to increase its capital to over [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C2%A3 "£")2.2 million(equivalent to £359.11 million in 2025)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-inflation-UK-50) through the enlarging of its stock by new subscriptions.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-51)

### 18th century

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/ONL_%281887%29_1.463_-_Dividend_Day_at_the_Bank%2C_1770.jpg/250px-ONL_%281887%29_1.463_-_Dividend_Day_at_the_Bank%2C_1770.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ONL_(1887)_1.463_-_Dividend_Day_at_the_Bank,_1770.jpg)

_[Dividend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dividend "Dividend") Day at the Bank, 1770_. The Pay Hall of 1732 was one of the Bank's first buildings on Threadneedle Street. (At one time shareholders were required to attend in person for the payment of Government dividends; the practice was abolished in 1910).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoEHistFun-25)

In 1700, the [Hollow Sword Blade Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollow_Sword_Blade_Company "Hollow Sword Blade Company") was purchased by a group of businessmen who wished to establish a competing English bank (in an action that would today be considered a "back door listing"). The Bank of England's initial monopoly on English banking was due to expire in 1710. However, it was instead renewed, and the Sword Blade company failed to achieve its goal.

The idea and reality of the [national debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_national_debt "United Kingdom national debt") came about at around this time, and this was also largely managed by the bank. Through the 1715 [Ways and Means](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ways_and_Means "Ways and Means") Act, Parliament authorised the bank to receive subscriptions for a government issue of 5% annuities, designed to raise £910,000;[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-52) this marked the start of the bank's role in managing Government Stocks, which were a means for people to invest in government debt (previously Government borrowing had been administered directly by the Exchequer).[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Hennessy1992-47) The bank was obliged by the Act to pay half-yearly [dividends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dividends "Dividends") and to keep a book record of all transfers (as it was already accustomed to do with regard to its own Bank Stock).

The bank did not have a monopoly on lending to the government, however: the [South Sea Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sea_Company "South Sea Company") had been established in 1711, and in 1720 it too became responsible for part of the UK's national debt, becoming a major competitor to the Bank of England. While the "South Sea Bubble" disaster soon ensued, the company continued managing part of the UK national debt until 1853. The [East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company "East India Company") too was a lender of choice for the government.

In 1734 there were ninety-six members of staff at the bank.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Hennessy1992-47) The bank's charter was renewed in 1742, and again in 1764. By the 1742 Act the bank became the only [joint-stock company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint-stock_company "Joint-stock company") allowed to issue bank notes in the metropolis.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-53)

#### Threadneedle Street

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/The_history_and_survey_of_London_-_from_its_foundation_to_the_present_time_%281756%29_%2814590189508%29.jpg/250px-The_history_and_survey_of_London_-_from_its_foundation_to_the_present_time_%281756%29_%2814590189508%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_history_and_survey_of_London_-_from_its_foundation_to_the_present_time_(1756)_(14590189508).jpg)

_A Perspective View of the Bank of England_ (published 1756). The bank initially occupied a narrow site on Threadneedle Street: behind the front building stood the [pedimented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedimented "Pedimented") Pay Hall, beyond which lay 'Bullion Court' (and the bank vaults below).

The Bank of England moved to its current location, on the site of Sir John Houblon's house and garden in [Threadneedle Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threadneedle_Street "Threadneedle Street") (close by the church of [St Christopher le Stocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Christopher_le_Stocks "St Christopher le Stocks")), in 1734.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Bldgs-54) (The estate had been purchased ten years earlier; Houblon had died in 1712, but his widow lived on in the house until her death in 1731, after which the house was demolished and work on the bank began.)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-BoE1794-1984-48)

The newly built premises, designed by George Sampson, occupied a narrow plot (around 80 feet (24 m) wide) extending north from Threadneedle Street.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-SoaneMusSampson-55) The front building contained [transfer offices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_transfer_agent "Stock transfer agent") on the first floor, beneath which was an entrance arch leading to a courtyard. Facing the entrance was the 'main building' of the bank:[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Maitland1756-56) a [large Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banking_hall "Banking hall") (24 m ×12 m; 79 ft ×40 ft) in which bank notes were issued and exchanged,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Phillips1805-57) and where deposits and withdrawals could be made.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Kynaston2017-42) (Sampson's Great Hall, later known as the Pay Hall, remained _in situ_ and in use until [Herbert Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Baker "Herbert Baker")'s comprehensive rebuilding in the late 1920s.)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Rebuilding-58) Beyond the Hall was a quadrangle of buildings enclosing a 'spacious and commodious Court-yard' (later known as Bullion Court). On the south side of the quadrangle were the Court Room and Committee Room, on the north side was a large Accountants' Office; on either side were [arcaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcaded "Arcaded") walkways, with rooms for the senior officers, while the upper floors contained offices and apartments.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-SoaneMusSampson-55) Beneath the quadrangle were the [vaults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_vault "Bank vault") ('that have very strong Walls and Iron Gates, for the Preservation of the Cash'); access to the courtyard was provided, by way of a passage leading to a 'grand Gateway' on Bartholomew Lane, for the coaches and waggons 'that come frequently loaded with Gold and Silver Bullion'.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Maitland1756-56) The pediment above the entrance to the main Hall was decorated with a carved _[alto relievo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto\_relievo "Alto relievo")_ figure of [Britannia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britannia "Britannia") (who had appeared on the [common seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_seal "Company seal") of the bank since 30 July 1694);[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-59) the sculptor was [Robert Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Taylor_(architect) "Robert Taylor (architect)"), who went on to be appointed Architect, in succession to Sampson, in 1764. Inside, the east end of the Hall was dominated by a large statue by [John Cheere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cheere "John Cheere") of [King William III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_III_of_England "William III of England"),[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-60) lauded in an accompanying Latin inscription as the bank's founder (_conditor_);[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Allen1828-49) at the opposite end, a large [Venetian window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venetian_window "Venetian window") looked out on St Christopher's churchyard.

#### Expansion

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/St_Christopher_le_Stocks.gif/250px-St_Christopher_le_Stocks.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Christopher_le_Stocks.gif)

The [Threadneedle Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threadneedle_Street "Threadneedle Street") front in 1773, after the addition of [Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Taylor_(architect) "Robert Taylor (architect)")'s east wing but before the demolition of [St Christopher le Stocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Christopher_le_Stocks "St Christopher le Stocks") (left)

In the second half of the 18th century the bank gradually acquired neighbouring plots of land to enable it to expand, and after 1765 new buildings began to be added by the bank's newly appointed architect Robert Taylor. North-west of the Pay Hall, overlooking St Christopher's churchyard to the south, Taylor built a suite of rooms for the Directors of the bank centred on a new (much larger) Court Room and Committee Room (When the bank was rebuilt in the 1920s-30s, these rooms were removed from their original ground-floor location and reconstructed on the first floor; they continue to be used for meetings of the bank's Court of Directors and Monetary Policy Committee respectively.).[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-62) East of the Pay Hall, Taylor built a suite of halls and offices dedicated to the management of stocks and dividends, which more or less doubled the size of the bank's footprint (extending it as far as Bartholomew Lane).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Kynaston2017-42) These rooms were centred on a large Rotunda, also known as the [Brokers' Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_exchange "Stock exchange"), where dealing in Government Stock took place; around it were arranged four sizeable Transfer Offices, each corresponding with a different fund (as described in the 1820s: 'In each office under the several letters of the alphabet, are arranged the books on which the names of all persons having property in the funds are registered, as well as the particulars of their respective interests').[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-Allen1828-49) All these offices were top-lit, to avoid the need for windows in the external walls.

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/A_view_of_the_Bank_of_England%2C_Threadneedle_Street%2C_London_%28NYPL_Hades-280166-1253467%29.tiff/lossy-page1-250px-A_view_of_the_Bank_of_England%2C_Threadneedle_Street%2C_London_%28NYPL_Hades-280166-1253467%29.tiff.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_view_of_the_Bank_of_England,_Threadneedle_Street,_London_(NYPL_Hades-280166-1253467).tiff)

The bank in 1797: matching east and west wings by [Sir Robert Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Robert_Taylor "Sir Robert Taylor") flank Sampson's centrepiece of 1733.

In 1782 the church of [St Christopher le Stocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Christopher_le_Stocks "St Christopher le Stocks") was demolished, allowing the bank to expand westwards along Threadneedle Street. The new west wing was completed to Taylor's design in 1786 (its frontage matching that of Taylor's earlier east wing): it housed the Reduced Annuities Office, the Cheque Office and the Dividend Warrant Office (among others). Immediately to the north lay the former churchyard of St Christopher le Stocks, which was preserved within the complex of buildings as a garden (known as the 'Garden Court'). North of Bullion Court, Taylor built a new four-storey Library, to house the bank's expanding collection of archives.

#### The Bank Picquet

The church's demolition had been prompted by the 1780 [Gordon Riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Riots "Gordon Riots"), during which rioters reportedly climbed on the church to throw projectiles at the buildings of the bank. During the riots, in June 1780, the Lord Mayor of London petitioned the Secretary of State to send a military guard to protect the bank and the Mansion House.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England#cite_note-63) Thenceforward a nightly guard (the '[Bank Picquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Picquet "Bank Picquet")') was provided by soldiers of the [Household Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household_Brigade "Household Brigade") (a practice which continued until 1973). To house the guard Taylor built a barracks (accessed from a separate entrance on Princes Street) in the north-west corner of the site.

**Burlington** is a [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_(New_Jersey) "City (New Jersey)") situated on the banks of the [Delaware River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River") in [Burlington County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_County,_New_Jersey "Burlington County, New Jersey"), in the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey"). It is a [suburb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburb "Suburb") of [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). As of the [2020 United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), the city's population was 9,743,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Census2020-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-LWD2020-11) a decrease of 177 (−1.8%) from the 9,920 recorded at the [2010 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census"),[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Census2010-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-LWD2010-21) which in turn reflected an increase of 184 (+1.9%) from the 9,736 counted in the [2000 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_census "2000 United States census").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-22) The city, and all of Burlington County, is a part of the [Philadelphia metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_metropolitan_area "Philadelphia metropolitan area").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-23)

Burlington was first incorporated on October 24, 1693, and was reincorporated by [Royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") on May 7, 1733. After American independence, the city was incorporated by the State of New Jersey on December 21, 1784. On March 14, 1851, the city was reincorporated and enlarged with portions of the surrounding township.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Story-24):94

Burlington was originally the county seat of Burlington County. In 1796, in response to the growth of population to the east away from the Delaware River, the county seat was moved to [Mount Holly Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Holly,_New_Jersey "Mount Holly, New Jersey"), a more central location.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-25)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The council of [West Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Jersey "West Jersey") Proprietors purchased roughly 30 miles (48 km) of riverfront land in 1676 from the [Lenape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape "Lenape")[Native Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States"). Burlington was founded on part of that land by English settlers (primarily [Quakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers "Quakers")) in 1677. It served as the capital of the province until 1702, when West Jersey and [East Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Jersey "East Jersey") were combined into a single [Crown Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Colony "Crown Colony").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-26)

Burlington takes its name (including the county name) from the town of [Bridlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridlington "Bridlington"), England of which Burlington was a district. It is now amalgamated into the larger Bridlington town.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-29)

The Quakers formally established their congregation in 1678. Initially, they met in private homes; between 1683 and 1687, Francis Collings constructed a hexagonal meeting house of brick. Over the next century, the membership grew substantially and a larger building was needed. The present meeting house on High Street was built in 1783 in front of the old meeting house and cemetery. The cemetery predated the first building. A tablet commemorates that the Lenape chief King Ockanickon, a loyal friend of the English settlers, was buried here in 1681. The oldest gravestone is inscribed "D.B. 1726." Many notable Quakers are buried here.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Intensive-30)

One of the oldest buildings in Burlington is known as the Revell House. Originally built in 1685 for George Hutchinson, it stood on East Pearl Street. The property was purchased by Thomas Revell, one of the original Anglo-European settlers. Local tradition associates this house with the young [Benjamin Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin "Benjamin Franklin"), who received gingerbread from the household while traveling from Boston to Philadelphia.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-31)

In the early 20th century, the house was purchased by the Annis Stockton Chapter of the [Daughters of the American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daughters_of_the_American_Revolution "Daughters of the American Revolution") for use as their clubhouse. The Colonial Burlington Foundation acquired and restored it in the 1950s.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Intensive-30)

### 18th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 18th century")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Old_St._Mary%27s_Church%2C_West_Broad_%26_Wood_Streets%2C_Burlington_%28Burlington_County%2C_New_Jersey%29.jpg/250px-Old_St._Mary%27s_Church%2C_West_Broad_%26_Wood_Streets%2C_Burlington_%28Burlington_County%2C_New_Jersey%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_St._Mary's_Church,_West_Broad_&_Wood_Streets,_Burlington_(Burlington_County,_New_Jersey).jpg)

The original [St. Mary's Episcopal church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary's_Episcopal_Church,_Burlington,_New_Jersey "St. Mary's Episcopal Church, Burlington, New Jersey"), built in 1703, the oldest church in New Jersey

Many institutions established in the 18th century continue to function in the 21st century. After the Quakers, the second oldest religious congregation in Burlington were the Anglicans (later known as Episcopalians). Their original church, Old St. Mary's, is the oldest church in Burlington and New Jersey. The congregation was founded in 1702 by George Keith and John Talbot. Talbot became the first minister and laid the cornerstone for the church in 1703. He served as the church's rector until 1725. The congregation prospered, and the church became the see of the Anglican bishops of New Jersey.

After the Revolution, the Episcopal Church in the United States was established. In 1846, under the leadership of Bishop and Rector [George Washington Doane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Doane "George Washington Doane"), construction was begun on New St. Mary's. This early [Gothic Revival architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_Revival_architecture "Gothic Revival architecture") church was designed by [Richard Upjohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Upjohn "Richard Upjohn"), who also designed [Trinity Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Church_(Manhattan) "Trinity Church (Manhattan)") at the foot of [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street "Wall Street") in [Lower Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Manhattan "Lower Manhattan").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-32) In the late 20th century, this building was designated as a [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") (NHL).

Bishop Doane founded an Episcopal girls' boarding school, St. Mary's, in Burlington in 1838, at a time when interest in girls' education led to development of schools for them in many areas. Girls from families up and down the East Coast came to study there, from as far as New England, Virginia, and upstate New York. St. Mary's provided a classical education, as well as classes in arts and music.

The Library Company of Burlington was organized in 1757 as a "free" library open to the public as well as members. There were 60 members of the original Library Company, each paying ten shillings per year to support the institution. The Library received a Charter from [George II of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_II_of_Great_Britain "George II of Great Britain") in 1758. The Library's books were kept in members' homes for a few years: Thomas Rodman's at 446 South High Street and, after 1767, Robert Smith's at 218 High Street. In 1789 the Library moved to its own building.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Intensive-30) In the early 21st century, the Library is housed in a stone building that was built on West Union Street in 1864. The Burlington Library is the oldest continuously operating library in New Jersey and the nation's seventh oldest.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-33)

The Endeavor Fire Company was organized in 1795. It was one of the four companies in the Burlington Fire Department when it was organized almost a century later. Endeavor was the first permanent firefighting organization in Burlington and remains one of the oldest fire companies under its original name in the state.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Shermerhorn-34) By 1882, the company had relocated to its present building, which was erected in 1852 as a Market House.

Burlington has been the home of many notable people including John Lawrence, a politician and his son, Captain [James Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lawrence "James Lawrence"). The elder Lawrence served in the State Assembly, as [Mayor of Burlington, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Burlington,_New_Jersey "Mayor of Burlington, New Jersey") in 1769, and as a member of the Provincial Council from 1771 to 1775. He was suspected of being a [Loyalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution) "Loyalist (American Revolution)") during the American Revolution, which ended his career. His son was born on October 1, 1781, and fought during the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-ship-35) Lawyer and writer [James Fenimore Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fenimore_Cooper "James Fenimore Cooper"), who wrote _[The Last of the Mohicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_of\_the\_Mohicans "The Last of the Mohicans")_, was also from Burlington. His father was a merchant there before buying land and developing [Cooperstown, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperstown,_New_York "Cooperstown, New York") after the Revolution.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-NYT2000-36)

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 19th century")]

As education for girls and young women became emphasized in the 19th century, Bishop George Washington Doane founded St. Mary's Hall in 1837 in association with the Episcopal diocese as the first Episcopal boarding school offering a classical education for girls and the first such school in New Jersey.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-37) In the 20th century, a boys' school was added. It is now known as [Doane Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doane_Academy "Doane Academy") and is a private, co-educational school for grades from Pre-K through 12th.

The building at 301 High Street houses the oldest continuously operating pharmacy in New Jersey. Originally a dwelling, the ground floor was converted to commercial use around 1845 by William Allinson, a druggist, local historian, and leading Quaker [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States "Abolitionism in the United States"). He used the building as a center of anti-slavery activity.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-38)[John Greenleaf Whittier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Greenleaf_Whittier "John Greenleaf Whittier") denounced slavery from the doorstep, and local tradition holds that fugitive slaves hid in tunnels under the building in their passage on the [Underground Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_Railroad "Underground Railroad"). New Jersey ended slavery, but many fugitives wanted to go farther north, beyond the reach of slave catchers.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Intensive-30)

[![Image 17: By Joshua Davidson / 2024](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/BNJUndergroundpainting.jpg/250px-BNJUndergroundpainting.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BNJUndergroundpainting.jpg)

A building painting of the underground railroad off Union Street

During the 19th century, Burlington City was known for the quality and quantity of its manufacturing. The shoe industry rivaled shipbuilding and canning in prominence.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Intensive-30) The [1850 United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1850_United_States_census "1850 United States census") indicates that the largest number of men were employed in the shoe industry, followed closely by carpentry and bricklaying. J. Frank Budd got his start in the shoe business at a Burlington shoe company just after the Civil War. In 1887, J.F. Budd broke ground for a children's "shoeworks" at the corner of Penn and Dilwyn streets. The company employed approximately 325 people and operated six days a week for ten hours a day. The J.F. Budd Baby Shoe Company billed itself as the "largest baby shoe plant in the world."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Shermerhorn-34)

The commercial activity provided revenues for the city's cultural activity. In 1839, a Lyceum was erected as a venue for lectures, concerts, and public meetings. It served in that capacity until 1851, when it was turned over to the city to be used as the City Hall. The municipal offices' move was concurrent with the adoption of a new City charter.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Shermerhorn-34)

The Oneida Boat Club was organized in 1873 by a group of 10 members. It is named for one of the original Five Nations of the [Iroquois Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iroquois_Confederacy "Iroquois Confederacy"), based in New York. Over the next few years, membership in the club grew rapidly. In 1876, they dedicated their newly built clubhouse on the banks of the Delaware River at York Street. The Oneida is the oldest continuously operating boat club located on the Delaware River.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Intensive-30)

During the 19th century, the City of Burlington developed in a grid pattern from the main crossroads of High and Broad streets. Blocks of attached rowhouses built in the latest architectural style characterize the city as a 19th-century town. Ferries carried traffic across the Delaware River to Pennsylvania before bridges were built.

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 20th century")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/BurlingtonNJ_Tourism_CarriageHouse.jpg/250px-BurlingtonNJ_Tourism_CarriageHouse.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BurlingtonNJ_Tourism_CarriageHouse.jpg)

This historic carriage house now houses the local tourism office in Burlington.

Burlington's waterfront park along the river was developed as a result of urban renewal and flood control projects in the late 1960s and 1970s. The shoreline improvements—revetments, walkways, etc.—span the city's Delaware riverfront from the [Burlington-Bristol Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington-Bristol_Bridge "Burlington-Bristol Bridge") to [Assiscunk Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assiscunk_Creek "Assiscunk Creek").

The remains of former waterfront industries, ferry terminals, and docks were demolished. Development of an open, grassy park with a tree-lined waterfront esplanade has reconnected city residents to the riverfront for recreation. This also ensures that business properties are not at risk during floods and reduces damages.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Intensive-30)

In this period, the United States federal and state governments began to value their historic assets more highly, and efforts were made to preserve structures that were significant to the layered history of places. In addition to recognition of individual structures, such as the [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") St. Mary's Church, the city has two historic districts listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places"), with multiple contributing buildings: the [Burlington Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_Historic_District_(Burlington,_New_Jersey) "Burlington Historic District (Burlington, New Jersey)") includes structures from both the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It is adjacent to the city's [High Street Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Street_Historic_District_(Burlington,_New_Jersey) "High Street Historic District (Burlington, New Jersey)").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-HistDistmap-39)

The Oneida Clubhouse narrowly escaped demolition during the urban renewal campaign. It was saved and renovated. As the new esplanade was built on fill that added land between the building and river's edge, it created a landlocked clubhouse for the boat club.

[Burlington Coat Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_Coat_Factory "Burlington Coat Factory") was founded in 1924 as a wholesaler of ladies' coats and outerwear. The modern company was formed in 1972 when Monroe Milstein purchased a warehouse in the outskirts of the city of Burlington. He started selling coats and outerwear there at discount prices. The company gradually added other apparel, including suits, shoes, and accessories, and has branched out to include baby items and linens, all at discount prices. The company's corporate headquarters was moved from the city to Burlington Township in 1988. The Burlington Coat Factory relocated to a new store site in the fall of 2008.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-40)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Geography")]

According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau"), the city had a total area of 3.78 square miles (9.79 km 2), including 3.06 square miles (7.93 km 2) of land and 0.72 square miles (1.87 km 2) of water (19.05%).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-CensusArea-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-GR1-2)

[Unincorporated communities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_government_in_New_Jersey#Unincorporated_communities "Local government in New Jersey"), localities and place names located partially or completely within the city include Burlington Island and East Burlington.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-41)

Burlington borders [Burlington Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_Township,_New_Jersey "Burlington Township, New Jersey") in Burlington County and both [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol,_Pennsylvania "Bristol, Pennsylvania") and [Bristol Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Township,_Bucks_County,_Pennsylvania "Bristol Township, Bucks County, Pennsylvania") across the [Delaware River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River") in [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-44)

The [Burlington-Bristol Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington-Bristol_Bridge "Burlington-Bristol Bridge") crosses the Delaware River, connecting Burlington to Bristol.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-BCBC-45)

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Government")]

### Local government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Local government")]

The City of Burlington is governed within the [Faulkner Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faulkner_Act "Faulkner Act") (formally known as the Optional Municipal Charter Law) under the [Mayor-Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faulkner_Act_(mayor%E2%80%93council) "Faulkner Act (mayor–council)") form of municipal government (Plan 4), implemented based on the recommendations of a [Charter Study Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_Study_Commission "Charter Study Commission") as of January 1, 1992.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-62) The city is one of 42 municipalities (of the 564) statewide that use this form of government.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-63) The governing body is comprised of the Mayor and the seven-member Common Council, all elected on a partisan basis in balloting held in odd-numbered years as part of the November general election.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-DataBook-3)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-64) The Mayor serves a four-year term of office. The Common Council is comprised of seven members, each serving four-year terms of office: three [at-large](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At-large "At-large") Councilmembers are elected to represent the entire city, while four are elected from [single-member districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-member_districts "Single-member districts"), known as [wards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ward_(United_States) "Ward (United States)").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-65) The three at-large and mayoral seats are up for election in one cycle, and the ward seats are elected together two years later.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-66)

As of 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit), the [Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor "Mayor") of Burlington City is [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") Barry W. Conaway, whose term of office ends December 31, 2027.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Mayor-4) Members of the Common Council are David H. Ballard (at-large; D, 2027), Dawn Bergner-Thompson (Ward 3; D, 2025 - elected to an unexpired term), George Chachis (Ward 1; D, 2025), Geneva Rijs (Ward 2; D, 2025 - appointed to serve an unexpired term), Xavier Roque (Ward 4; D, 2025), Richard Spaulding (at-large; D, 2027) and Suzanne Johnson Woodard (at-large; D, 2027).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Burlington2023-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Burlington2022-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Burlington2021-71)

In February 2024, the common council appointed Geneva Rijs to fill the Ward 2 seat expiring in December 2025 that had been held by J. Roosevelt Smith until he resigned from office the previous month; Rijs will serve on an interim basis until the November 2024 general election, when voters will choose a candidate to serve the balance of the term of office.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-72)

In April 2022, Dawn Bergner-Thompson was appointed to the Ward 3 seat expiring in December 2025 that had been held by Helen Hatala until she died the previous month.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-73) Bergner-Thompson served on an interim basis until the November 2022 general election, when she was elected to serve the balance of the term of office.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-Burlington2022-70)

In January 2016, the City Council appointed George Chachis to fill the Ward 1 seat expiring in 2017 that had been held by Barry Conaway until he was appointed as mayor.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-74)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Education")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/BurlingtonNJ_WilliamRAllenSchool.jpg/250px-BurlingtonNJ_WilliamRAllenSchool.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BurlingtonNJ_WilliamRAllenSchool.jpg)

The historic [William R. Allen School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._Allen_School "William R. Allen School") was originally built for the education of black children.

The [City of Burlington Public School District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Burlington_Public_School_District "City of Burlington Public School District") serves students in [pre-kindergarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-kindergarten "Pre-kindergarten") through [twelfth grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelfth_grade "Twelfth grade").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-114) The district is one of 31 former [Abbott districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbott_district "Abbott district") statewide that were established pursuant to the decision by the [New Jersey Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Supreme_Court "New Jersey Supreme Court") in _Abbott v. Burke_[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-115) which are now referred to as "SDA Districts" based on the requirement for the state to cover all costs for school building and renovation projects in these districts under the supervision of the [New Jersey Schools Development Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Schools_Development_Authority "New Jersey Schools Development Authority").[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-116)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-117) As of the 2020–21 school year, the district, comprised of four schools, had an enrollment of 1,740 students and 170.9 classroom teachers (on an [FTE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full-time_equivalent "Full-time equivalent") basis), for a [student–teacher ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student%E2%80%93teacher_ratio "Student–teacher ratio") of 10.2:1.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-NCES-118) The schools in the district (with 2020–21 enrollment data from the [National Center for Education Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Center_for_Education_Statistics "National Center for Education Statistics")[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-119)) are Captain James Lawrence Elementary School[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-120) with 238 students in grades Pre-K–2, Samuel Smith Elementary School[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-121) with 281 students in grades Pre-K–2, Wilbur Watts Intermediate School[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-122) with 444 students in grades 3–6 and [Burlington City High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_City_High_School "Burlington City High School")[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-123) with 727 students in grades 7–12.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-124)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-125) In 2018, the district closed Elias Boudinot Elementary School, which had served grades K–2, citing declining enrollment, the opportunities to reduce costs and the potential to raise funds by selling the site.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-126) The district's high school serves as a receiving school for students in grade nine through twelve from [Edgewater Park Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgewater_Park,_New_Jersey "Edgewater Park, New Jersey"), as part of a [sending/receiving relationship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sending/receiving_relationship "Sending/receiving relationship") with the [Edgewater Park School District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgewater_Park_School_District "Edgewater Park School District").[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-127)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-128)

Students from Burlington City, and from all of Burlington County, are eligible to attend the [Burlington County Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_County_Institute_of_Technology "Burlington County Institute of Technology"), a countywide public school district that serves the vocational and technical education needs of students at the high school and post-secondary level at its campuses in [Medford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medford,_New_Jersey "Medford, New Jersey") and [Westampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westampton,_New_Jersey "Westampton, New Jersey").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-129)

[Doane Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doane_Academy "Doane Academy"), a co-educational, Episcopal college-preparatory school, was founded as St. Mary's Hall, a boarding school for girls, by [George Washington Doane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Doane "George Washington Doane") in 1837. The name was shortened from St. Mary's Hall-Doane Academy in March 2008.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-130) All Saints Catholic Grade School (Pre-K though 8th grade) closed in June 2006 with several other Catholic schools in the [Roman Catholic Diocese of Trenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Trenton "Roman Catholic Diocese of Trenton") due to low enrollment, after 75 years of operation, based on recommendations issued in 2005 to help improve diocese finances.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-131)

St. Paul Grammar School serves students in grades PreK-8 and operates under the auspices of the [Roman Catholic Diocese of Trenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Trenton "Roman Catholic Diocese of Trenton").[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-132)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-133)

### Roads and highways

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Roads and highways")]

As of May 2010[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burlington,_New_Jersey&action=edit), the city had a total of 42.76 miles (68.82 km) of roadways, of which 35.71 miles (57.47 km) were maintained by the municipality, 4.36 miles (7.02 km) by Burlington County, 2.30 miles (3.70 km) by the [New Jersey Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Department_of_Transportation "New Jersey Department of Transportation"), and 0.39 miles (0.63 km) by the [Burlington County Bridge Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_County_Bridge_Commission "Burlington County Bridge Commission").[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-134)

Main roads directly serving Burlington include [U.S. Route 130](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_130 "U.S. Route 130"), [New Jersey Route 413](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Route_413 "New Jersey Route 413"), [County Route 541](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Route_541_(New_Jersey) "County Route 541 (New Jersey)") and [County Route 543](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Route_543_(New_Jersey) "County Route 543 (New Jersey)").[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-135)[Interstate 95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_95_in_New_Jersey "Interstate 95 in New Jersey"), [Interstate 295](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_295_(Delaware_%E2%80%93_New_Jersey) "Interstate 295 (Delaware – New Jersey)") and the [New Jersey Turnpike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Turnpike "New Jersey Turnpike") all pass fairly close to the city and are easily accessible from Burlington.

The [Burlington-Bristol Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington-Bristol_Bridge "Burlington-Bristol Bridge"), part of Route 413, crosses the [Delaware River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River"), connecting Burlington to [Bristol Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Township,_Pennsylvania "Bristol Township, Pennsylvania"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), and is operated by the Burlington County Bridge Commission. Construction of the bridge started on April 1, 1930, and the bridge opened to traffic on May 1, 1931.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey#cite_note-BCBC-45) The bridge carries NJ 413 and [Pennsylvania Route 413](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Route_413 "Pennsylvania Route 413").
